# Units, Datums, and Real Lumber

Most CAD mistakes are not modeling mistakes. They are unit mistakes, datum
mistakes, or assumptions about material that is not the size the drawing says.
This chapter sets the conventions that the rest of the book uses.

## What you will learn

- Why the book models in millimetres.
- The difference between nominal and actual lumber.
- How to choose a datum that survives a design change.
- How to treat tolerance and material movement as design input.

## Why millimetres

Woodworking happens at the millimetre scale. A 1 mm error is visible in a joint;
a 0.1 mm error usually is not. Working in one unit removes a whole class of
conversion errors, especially when hardware dimensions are metric and lumber
dimensions are not.

SolidCraft can display mm, cm, m, inches, or feet. The display unit changes how
values are shown; it does not change the model. Pick mm for this book and stay
with it unless a supplier's drawing forces something else.

::: {.callout-tip}
If a dimension looks ten times too large or too small, check the display unit
before editing geometry. Converting the model to "fix" a unit display is a
classic way to create a real error.
:::

## Nominal is not actual

A "2 × 4" is a name, not a size. In North American softwood construction the
actual dressed size is smaller. The table below is an example, not a universal
standard; metric timber, hardwoods, and imported stock follow different rules.

| Nominal | Actual (mm) | Common use |
|---------|-------------|------------|
| 2 × 4 | 38 × 89 | studs, rails, blocking |
| 2 × 6 | 38 × 140 | joists, deck boards, rails |
| 2 × 8 | 38 × 184 | joists, beams |
| 2 × 10 | 38 × 235 | joists, beams |
| 2 × 12 | 38 × 286 | joists, headers |
| 4 × 4 | 89 × 89 | posts |
| 6 × 6 | 140 × 140 | heavier posts |

The habit that matters is: **model the actual size, record the nominal name.**
If you model a 2 × 4 as 50 × 100 mm, every joint, gap, and cut list will be
wrong by a few millimetres, and those millimetres accumulate.

## Choose a datum

A datum is the reference from which dimensions are measured. Good datums are
easy to find on site and unlikely to move when the design changes.

Useful choices:

- the outside face of a corner post;
- the top of a finished deck;
- the ground line at the high side of a sloped site;
- the centreline of a wall or fence run.

Avoid using the centre of a board that might change size later, or a decorative
edge that a future feature might cut away. Write the datum down in the chapter
or in a design note. "Origin at the outside corner of the north-east post, top
of post at Z = 1800" is much better than "origin at the corner."

## Tolerances are part of the design

CAD geometry is exact. Wood is not. A model that assumes two boards occupy the
same space will look fine on screen and fail on site.

A practical starting point:

- **1–2 mm** clearance for a joint that should slide together or a part that
  must not bind.
- **3–5 mm** allowance for site layout and framing tolerances.
- **3–6 mm** gaps between deck boards, following the manufacturer's guidance
  for the material and climate.
- A visible expansion gap wherever a panel, board, or gate meets something
  that will not move.

These are starting values, not rules. Your tools, species, moisture content,
and climate decide the real number.

## Measure the site, not the drawing

Before modeling an existing wall, deck, or fence line, measure the actual
condition. Record:

- overall length and width at more than one place;
- diagonals, to detect out-of-square;
- the difference in ground height across the footprint;
- the location of doors, windows, downspouts, utilities, and obstructions;
- any slope or camber in an existing surface.

Put those measurements into parameters early. A model built on a guessed 4000
mm site will not survive contact with a 3965 mm reality.

## Build along: a rail with the right section

1. Set the design units to mm.
2. Make a 45 × 140 mm rectangle, with the 140 mm face vertical.
3. Extrude it 2400 mm.
4. Place the bottom at Z = 0 and the outside face at Y = 0.
5. Save it as `designs/02-rail.solidcraft`.

Then change the display unit to inches and back to mm. Confirm that the
geometry did not move.

## Checks

- The rail's bounding box is 45 × 140 × 2400 mm.
- The 140 mm dimension is vertical, not horizontal.
- The datum faces are the ones you would measure from on site.
- The nominal name ("2 × 6") is recorded somewhere, even though the model uses
  38 × 140 mm.

## Exercises

1. Model a 38 × 89 mm stud, 2400 mm long.
2. Model a 19 × 140 mm deck board, 3000 mm long, with a 5 mm gap to its
   neighbour. What is the pitch from one board to the next?
3. Measure a board in your shop. Compare its actual dimensions with the nominal
   name and with the table above.

## Next

With units and datums under control, you can start drawing profiles. The next
chapter is about sketches that behave predictably when you change them.
